title: On one foot (Shabbat 31a)
hookLine: a man asks Hillel for the whole Torah on one foot: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor; go and learn

lines: WHILE I STAND ON ONE FOOT.
cards: Give me the short version. Explain your job in one sentence. Sum up the whole book in a tweet.
It's usually a little impatient, and a little unfair. Long ago, a man who wasn't Jewish walked up to Hillel, one of the great sages of his day, and made an impatient request.
Teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot. Everything. Before I lose my balance.
Today, what Hillel said, and the line after it that often gets dropped.

teach.b: The story is in the Talmud, tractate Shabbat, page 31a. The man says he'll convert if Hillel can teach him the whole Torah while he stands on one foot. Hillel doesn't laugh or send him away.

teach.h: DON'T DO IT TO YOUR NEIGHBOR.
teach.b: He accepts him, and says, in Aramaic: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah.
Go and learn it. Three moves. First, the rule.
It echoes the Torah's own words, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself," from Leviticus. But Hillel turns it into something anyone can check. You may not always know what love asks of you.
You almost always know what hurts. Start there.

Second: the rest is commentary. Hillel doesn't say the rest doesn't matter. The Sabbath, the festivals, the food laws, the prayers: he calls all of it the explanation, that one rule worked out in real life.
Third, the part people drop: go and learn. The summary fits on one foot. Living it takes both feet and the rest of your life.

Hillel gives the man a door, not a shortcut. And notice who he says it to: an outsider, impatient, maybe a little rude. The whole Torah on one foot is also a lesson in how to answer a question like that.

how: Hillel's answer is often taught to children, quoted in sermons, and paired with the Torah's command to love your neighbor as yourself.

o: the outsider who asked for the Torah in a hurry
a king of Judea in the days of the sages
a sage who summed up the Torah on one foot

games.q: Hillel's answer, in three moves — tap the pairs.
p: the whole Torah on one foot

s: Hillel said the rest of the Torah doesn't matter
he called it commentary, the working-out of the rule, and said go and learn it.
Hillel's rule echoes Leviticus: love thy neighbor as thyself
he puts it in a form anyone can check: don't do what hurts you.
the man who asked was not Jewish
he wanted to convert, and asked for the whole Torah on one foot.

games.q: you're a teacher. a stranger says: teach me your whole tradition while I stand on one foot. what do you do?
o: send him away. it's a rude question.
give him one sentence, then: go and learn.
tell him it can't be summed up.
games.why: Hillel gave him one sentence, what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor, and then sent him to learn the rest.

practice: Think of one thing that really stings when someone does it to you: being interrupted, being talked about, being left on read, being corrected in front of people.
Picture the moment in your day when you might be tempted to do that same thing to someone else. Then see yourself not doing it; that's Hillel's rule, lived for one day.

wordCard.voice: Hillel, who agreed to teach the whole Torah while a man stood on one foot: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor. The rest is commentary. Go and learn.

orig.note: Aramaic: go and learn. the last words of Hillel's answer.

carryVoice: Your line: the rest is commentary. One rule on one foot, and a lifetime of learning after it. Until tomorrow.
